Done. PTAL. :)

Yeah, so the worker event loop changes seems incorrect. In particular, you run the substeps for each task processed by a worker, whereas you only want to run them sometimes, say, at 60Hz.

In particular, you want something like substep 3 of "Update the rendering" (the one for documents) where you do an early return if the worker does not require a rendering update. And there you want to attach the note.

Is this logic of when you skip a rendering update for a worker tied to its owners by the way? If it has an owner document that is not displayed, is it valid to not give it rendering updates?

Should this be exposed in service workers by the way? This API does not make much sense to me there given how it be quit early and such.

Gotcha! :)
I cleared up all references to WorkerGlobalScope to be DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope. (which clears the ServiceWorker thing).
And I think I understood what you meant by the event loop thing and fixed it.
All done. :)

Where is the `commit()` aspect of the change proposal? As far as I can tell all it does thus far is making `requestAnimationFrame()` available in a dedicated worker.

How does it relate btw that `OffscreenCanvas` is available in all workers? Isn't that problematic?

Anne, good point. I had the commit changes here, but I somehow split them when sending. Is it ok if I leave this as only the RAF and send a separate one for commit?

OffscreenCanvas works fine with other types of workers. The commit/renderloop changes are only needed for OffscreenCanvases that are "transferedToOffscreen" from a regular canvas (i.e., that are sent to DedicatedWorker). For cases where an OffscreenCanvas is just posted back and forth, there's no need for the commit/render loop changes, so everything should work fine. Does this make sense?

Yeah, we could discuss `commit()` changes in a separate PR, but I suspect we want to land them around the same time.

Do you mean `transferControlToOffscreen()`? What prevents such an `OffscreenCanvas` object from being transferred to a non-dedicated worker?

Review status: this needs various editorial changes to comply with the formatting guidelines, as well as rebasing on top of #3707 once that lands so it can use the same underlying concept rather than invoking `now()` directly (that step also needs to be made conditional upon the event loop being for a dedicated worker). Otherwise I think it's mostly fine.

Yes, I'll send a `commit()` one soon.

For the `transferControlToOffscreen()`, yes. Nothing prevents it yet on the spec, as far as I understand.
I'd claim that without a `DedicatedWorker`, the only way a `OffscreenCanvas` can be updated is with a direct `commit()` (the new blocking one). This RAF + rendering event loop model just allows `DedicatedWorker` to make `OffscreenCanvas` behave nicely.
I'll give a try at the formatting guidelines, although I thought the linter got them all. I can easily update to #3707 once it lands.

Thanks to a blink-dev thread I realized there's another fundamental problem here. This only works for dedicated workers that belong to an agent cluster that also contains a window. If a shared or service worker creates a dedicated worker none of this should work.

I wonder if that means we need additional IDL machinery to hide the APIs there? At the very least we need to add more conditionals.

Implementation bugs:

[Edge](https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/platform/issues/17934399/)
[Firefox](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1469282)
[Safari](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=186760)
Chrome already implements it.
Would it be possible for us to address the new worker situation in a separate PR? Or do you think we need to do this here?

Ideally we do it here as it also affects API exposure and what this API needs to do in dedicated workers that are not equipped to handle this.

(As with software we try to keep the master branch somewhat clean and have each individual commit result in something that works.)

Do you think we could limit this by saying that `requestAnimationFrame` is available on `DedicatedWorkers` that are created from a `window` object"` and should throw an exception when that's not the case?

This way we don't need new IDL mechanisms, although it's a bit ugly.

@fserb so you don't want to support window -> dedicated worker -> dedicated worker? I think that should work as that's all the same agent cluster. I'd rather not introduce yet another boundary.

It seems somewhat okay to not have a new IDL boundary, but we should maybe ask more people for opinions since as far as I know it's a new thing (though maybe other APIs already did this?).

I wouldn't mind that those be included, I was just suggesting that we could address this outside IDL changes.

That said, Do you feel that `agent cluster` is the right abstraction for that? Let me try without it. Let's see how it looks.
What do you think about this solution?

That doesn't define:

* when it's tagged "invalid"
* scope
* the exception to be thrown
* an exception for the second method

I'm pretty sure that an agent cluster that contains a similar-origin window agent is the boundary we want here, however we define it. What I'd like input from others on is whether exposing the API on dedicated workers outside that boundary is acceptable, even though we'll likely never make them work.

cc @domenic

I've defined the exceptions on both methods. For the "when/scope", you think this is not enough? ```

An AnimationFrameProvider implementation is marked as invalid if the object that includes it was created from a scope that doesn't implement a valid AnimationFrameProvider. ```

No, that doesn't build upon any primitives.

As for the exception, if I understand your intent correctly you want to copy-and-paste the style used for `"NotSupportedError" DOMException` elsewhere.
Changed the DOMException. Also changed the "invalid" to "not supported" to mirror the exception. I'm not sure what you meant by "built upon primitives". Could you help me here?

The current definition makes it sound like it's implementation defined when something is "not supported". Instead, it should be tied to the agent/agent cluster or traversing the worker's global's owner set.

I thought it would be enough to make it "recursive" like that:

```
An AnimationFrameProvider implementation is considered not supported if the object that
includes it was created from a scope that doesn't implement a supported 
AnimationFrameProvider. AnimationFrameProvider must be supported on Window.
```

I was trying to avoid adding the concept of agent cluster from Ecma. But it seems `worker's owner set` is a thing. So maybe I can try that too.
@fserb agent cluster and similar-origin window agent and other terms I've been using are already a thing in HTML. The problem with your definition is that it doesn't define "scope".
Does `execution context` works here instead?
I don't see how. It doesn't seem to follow from this definition on what dedicated workers it functions?

If the `DedicatedWorker` was created from a `Window` or from another `DedicatedWorker` that had a valid `requestAnimationFrame` then it will have. If a `DedicatedWorker` was created from a Service Worker, then it won't, because the execution context of the Service Worker doesn't have `requestAnimationFrame`.
That doesn't work as the object that includes `AnimationFrameProvider` is the global of the dedicated worker and that's not created by the global of the `Window` object.

okey.

I don't understand how to phrase this in terms of `owner set` because the `Document` is part of it, not the `Window`. Would it be enough to say that if the `owner set` contains a `Document` then the `DedicatedWork` must support `AnimationFrameProvider`?

Yeah, but you need to make it recursive. If owner set only contains dedicated workers you want to look at their owners. I guess you can bail out if you have multiple owners too.

I think a more ideal solution would be that we introduce "current agent cluster" and we do a check based on that, maybe file a follow-up on that? Seems useful if this becomes more widespread.
I gave it a try at the `owner set` language. PTAL.

Thanks, I think that works, but it could use some editorial work that @domenic is hopefully willing to pick up. I'll be out for 3.5 weeks. I'm happy to pick this up when I'm back and try to finish it up if he doesn't get to it though. Note that I also wrote https://github.com/w3ctag/design-reviews/issues/288#issuecomment-398672236 to see if we could get some additional review on the overall implications here, but no feedback thus far.

Do workers attached to background windows fire rAF callbacks in the worker?

AIUI at least a few browsers do not fire rAF callbacks for background windows on the main thread.  Also, there is a desire to throttle background workers in general.

I see the spec has vague wording about "the user agent believes that it would benefit from having its rendering updated", but it was unclear to me if in practice this background throttling would apply to these workers.

Also, it would be good to have a small bit of sample code, showing how to use the worker's requestAnimationFrame, in the spec. I think that will be non-obvious to many readers, since this section never mentions any connection with OffscreenCanvas. (Which I assume is how this is all connected?)
@wanderview, in practice the UA will apply the same background throttling to these workers.
